rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2014> two-year field experiment (2008, 2009) on sandy soil at Sarabuim, Egypt, randomized block factorial with surface vs subsurface drip and four irrigation levels. Q2: Results 'Yield and Yield Components', Table 2 <U+2014> subsurface drip at 80% ETc gave yield and yield components comparable to surface drip at full supply; subsurface drip averaged 36.32 t/ha vs 30.18 t/ha for surface drip (20.4% increase). Q4: 'Soil Water Distribution', Fig. 1 <U+2014> gravimetric soil moisture sampled to 70 cm depth and 35 cm radius; subsurface drip kept >16% water content down to 40 cm (the root zone), which the authors link to the higher yield. Q7: Results discussion <U+2014> authors state that higher yield can be achieved by placing the drip line sufficiently below the soil surface so water reaches the active root zone; the 20% saving without yield loss is reported only for the buried line.
rows.notes: The passage attributes a tomato result at 80% of field capacity to Badr et al. (2010); this study is on potato (cv. Cara) with irrigation levels expressed as % ETc, not % field capacity, so the review appears to have cited the wrong Badr et al. 2010 paper (the tomato fertigation paper is in this study's reference list). Rated on what this study reports: drip (surface and subsurface) and tuber yield. Q3: yield from harvest sampling only, single method. Q5/Q6: one site, one soil, one crop, 4.5 x 10 m plots. Q8: no limitations stated. Q9: Table 2 gives LSD(5%) values only, which is a significance threshold rather than a dispersion measure; no SD/SE/CI reported, so rated no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2014> own two-season field experiment on potato with surface and subsurface drip at 100/80/60/40% ETc. Q2: Results 'Yield and Yield Components' and 'Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency', Table 3 <U+2014> reducing water to 80% ETc under subsurface drip gave yield comparable to surface drip at full supply, indicating 20% of irrigation water can be saved; subsurface drip had higher WUE at all levels (e.g. 212 vs 138 kg/ha/mm at 40% ETc in 2008). Q4: Fig. 1 and 'Soil Water Distribution' <U+2014> measured soil water profiles show a dry surface (~12%) under subsurface drip and more water retained in the 0<U+2013>40 cm root zone, the pathway through which evaporation loss is reduced. Q7: Results <U+2014> authors state the saving/yield benefit requires the drip line to be buried sufficiently below the surface (here 15 cm in sandy soil) so capillary rise to the surface is restricted.
rows.notes: Same mis-attribution as row 17: the study is on potato, not tomato, and the 80% level is % ETc rather than % field capacity. Water saving is inferred from applied-water amounts and yield, not from measured evaporation or drainage. Q3: single method (applied water vs yield). Q5/Q6: single site, soil, crop, plot scale. Q8: no limitations given. Q9: Table 3 (WUE) reports means only, no LSD, SD, SE or CI.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2014> field experiment, 2008 and 2009, surface vs subsurface drip, potato on sandy soil. Q2: 'Water and Fertilizer Use Efficiency', Table 3 and Conclusions <U+2014> subsurface drip recorded higher WUE than surface drip at all irrigation levels, maximum at 40% ETc; 'Soil Water Distribution' <U+2014> water under subsurface drip remained in the root zone and was not lost to deep percolation. Q4: Fig. 1 <U+2014> gravimetric soil moisture mapped by depth and radial distance at four growth stages, showing the dry surface layer and wetter 0<U+2013>40 cm zone under subsurface drip that the authors use to explain reduced evaporation and higher WUE. Q7: Results <U+2014> authors state the benefit depends on placing the drip line sufficiently below the soil surface within the root level; line was set at 15 cm because of the low capillary forces of sandy soil.
rows.notes: The study supports the WP/WUE part of the passage with its own data. Reduced soil evaporation is inferred from surface moisture, not measured directly; reduced deep seepage is inferred from moisture profiles only (no drainage measurement). Q3: WUE from one method (yield / applied water). Q5/Q6: single sandy site, single crop, plot scale; the context sentence's claim that effects vary with soil and climate is not something this study tests. Q8: no limitations stated. Q9: Table 3 reports WUE means with no dispersion measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2014> own two-season field experiment on potato with surface and subsurface drip.
rows.notes: The study does not measure or report weed growth or any pest/weed outcome. The only mention of weed control is in the Introduction, citing other work (Enciso et al. 2005; Lamm and Camp 2007; Selim et al. 2009) that a dry surface under subsurface drip improves weed control. What the study actually shows is soil water distribution, potato yield, WUE and FUE under surface vs subsurface drip at four irrigation levels.

notes: Full text appears complete. The review LIT_0038 cites this paper for a tomato result that is not in it; this study is on potato and the authors' tomato fertigation paper (Badr et al. 2010, Healthy Plants 62:11<U+2013>19) is a separate publication. Statistics reported are ANOVA with LSD(5%) for yield (Table 2) and R2 for the water<U+2013>yield regression (Fig. 2); no SD, SE or CI anywhere.
